source.title: Iterative Label Refinement Matters More than Preference Optimization under Weak Supervision
source.authors: Yaowen Ye; Cassidy Laidlaw; Jacob Steinhardt

page_placements.theme: A generative policy ends up preferred over its own weaker supervisor (an LLM judge or time-limited humans)

record.file_problem: None apparent; the paper text includes the main sections and appendices.
record.tranche_reason: Tests weak-to-strong generalization by fine-tuning larger language models on smaller-model-generated demonstrations, but uses text-generation tasks and does not calculate Burns et al.'s PGR measure.
record.gate_note: Figure 2 reports the weak-supervisor versus larger SFT model results, and the text explicitly says the larger models outperform their supervisors. The paper also says ground-truth-trained SFT models outperform the weak-demonstration SFT models, so the recovery is incomplete. Figure 2 values are not given in extractable text. DPO/ILR comparisons and the DPO-variant tables are not recorded as rows: they concern the paper's preference-optimization/refinement methods and do not measure PGR or the weak-to-strong SFT comparison. The human study's preference results are recorded under fits_no_version because its supervisor is time-constrained humans, not a weaker model.
record.test_reason: In four LM-supervised settings (Gemma 2B→Mistral 7B and Mistral 7B→Llama 3 70B on GSM8K, 2B→70B on BIRD, 2B→7B on SaferPaca), the study fine-tunes a larger model on a smaller model's generated demonstrations. It compares the result with the supervisor and with a ground-truth-trained ceiling, extending the Burns et al. setup to text generation (Figure 2). It also compares training changes on top of weak-label SFT (DPO, IPO/cDPO/rDPO, ILR, naive self-relabelling) that use only weak-model supervision. PGR is not computed numerically.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that SFT on unreliable demonstrations beats the demonstrations' source (weak-to-strong generalization) but falls well short of ground-truth SFT. They find DPO fails to improve beyond SFT under unreliable supervision, which they attribute to overoptimization versus KL regularization. ILR, which uses comparison feedback to replace demonstrations, outperforms DPO in LM-simulated and human settings.
record.recipe_differences: Uses the weak-to-strong setup of training a larger pretrained model on a smaller model's generated labels, but applies it to text-generation tasks rather than the classification setting described for Burns et al.; it does not compute PGR.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that ILR improvements vary with model size and task, and that human participants choose fewer AI proposals in later refinement rounds.

fits_no_version.finding: In both ILR rounds, time-constrained human raters were at least moderately confident in preferring a model's proposal over the human demonstration it was trained on in more than 20% of questions, with fewer AI picks in round 2.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Models fine-tuned on unreliable human demonstrations can produce outputs that human supervisors prefer to their own, i.e. weak-to-strong generalization with a human supervisor.

fits_no_version.finding: With time-constrained human demonstrations and feedback on Alpaca, SFT+ILR improves over SFT on human demonstrations while DPO plateaus (Figure 6c).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Label refinement helps more than preference optimization under unreliable human supervision.

record.problems: The paper does not report numerical PGR. Figure 2 values are only available in plots in the supplied text, with no uncertainty estimates stated for those results. The weak-supervision experiments cover four task/model pairings and use LM-simulated supervisors; the paper's human study uses time-constrained human supervision instead.
record.rows_left_out: No rows left out under the 60-row limit. DPO-versus-ILR results and DPO-variant tables are omitted because they compare preference/refinement methods and do not report the weak-to-strong SFT PGR or the weak-supervisor-to-SFT outcome.

untested.parts: No numeric PGR or per-setting uncertainty for the weak-to-strong SFT comparison; classification tasks are not used.
Auxiliary confidence loss and ensembling of weak supervisors are not tested. Method comparisons are reported as accuracy gains over the weak-label SFT model, not as PGR.
No numeric PGR across sizes or tasks, no representation-based predictors, no chess or reward modelling. Task and size pairs vary, but the study does not report how the gap recovered varies with them.
No distribution shift, exploitation of unchecked errors, or error-similarity analysis.

missing.what: Accuracy of SFT+ILR vs SFT+DPO vs the round-0 weak-label SFT model in each of the four settings (method gains over naive weak-label fine-tuning)
GSM8K 2B→7B accuracies for DPO, sDPO, wsDPO, IPO, cDPO, rDPO and ILR over rounds 1–4
Naive ILR (replacing labels with student outputs without feedback) degrades performance on all tasks
DPO with oracle vs unreliable feedback starting from the weak-label SFT model; effect of KL coefficient β

record.verdict_notes: The rows' V3 links and both V3 labels were dropped. Without numeric PGR, the study only shows a positive gap in every setting, not how it varies. Incomplete recovery (PGR<1) is consistent with the original paper and does not qualify V1. V2 is tested in a broad sense: the training changes use weak-model comparison feedback (q̃, built on the same small model) rather than the specific methods named in Burns et al. The V2 verdicts rest on text and figures that no row records. Figure 2 values are not extractable.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not calculate PGR numerically or report its uncertainty.

It does not test the listed weak-to-strong training changes (such as auxiliary confidence loss or ensembling weak supervisors) against naive weak-label fine-tuning using PGR. Its DPO loss variants are preference-optimization methods, not tests of that PGR claim.
It varies task and supervisor/student size, but does not calculate PGR, test representation-based predictors, or study chess or reward modelling.
No test of distribution shift, unchecked student exploitation, or error similarity between weak and strong models.
No theoretical conditions for a student to outperform its supervisor.
No vision or other non-language modality.

statements.correction: Figure 2 includes the same student trained on ground-truth demonstrations as a strong ceiling in all four LM-supervised settings; Section 4 states that it significantly outperforms weak-demonstration SFT. Exact comparison values are figure-only.
statements.problem: The supervisor comparison is correct, but the claim that this study reports no strong ceiling is false.

statements.correction: Figure 4: ILR improves over round-0 weak-label SFT across four LM-supervised settings. Appendix E.4, Table 2: GSM8K Gemma 2B→Mistral 7B ILR accuracy at round 3 = 0.3851. Abstract: code and data available. Supplied source: arXiv v1, 14 January 2025, marked Preprint.
statements.problem: The performance claims and code availability are supported; ICLR review status cannot be verified from the supplied text, which identifies itself as a preprint.

statements.correction: Section 4: DPO fails to improve weak-label SFT with unreliable comparison feedback. Tables 2–3: GSM8K 2B→7B DPO accuracy = 0.3591 at DPO round 1 and 0.3412 at round 4; 0.3591 is not the initial SFT baseline. Appendix E.5: robust losses remain ineffective for this unreliable-supervision setting. V2 label for the stated failure condition: challenges.
statements.problem: The empirical claims are correct, but the limits_scope label understates explicitly absent or reversed method gains under the named conditions.

statements.correction: Section 5.2 and Appendix E.2, Figure 9: replacing an alpha fraction of labels with model proposals without comparison feedback degrades performance in four settings: GSM8K 2B→7B, GSM8K 7B→70B, BIRD 2B→70B, and SaferPaca 2B→7B.
statements.problem: Naive ILR degradation is supported, but there are three tasks across four settings, not four tasks.

statements.correction: Section 5.1: proposal models train on disjoint data halves and generate proposals for the half they did not train on. Section 6: moderately or strongly preferred AI proposals exceed 20% in both rounds. Figure 6b: round-2 frequencies include only pairs with at least one human-written label; fewer AI responses are selected later. Figure 6c: ILR improves over initial SFT; weakly regularized DPO initially improves then plateaus.
statements.problem: The percentage and improvement claims are supported, but cross-labelling means the proposal model was not trained on the paired demonstration; the round-2 denominator also needs qualification.
